Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Archival Storage
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Archival Storage and Hybrid Cloud Solutions

Learn how to select S3 Glacier tiers for long retention, set lifecycle transitions for automated archiving, and use Storage Gateway to bridge on-premises systems to AWS storage without rearchitecting applications.

Concept Map
Glacier tiers, lifecycle policies, Storage Gateway
S3 Glacier
Low-cost archival with configurable retrieval speeds.
Deep Archive
Lowest-cost tier for years-long retention.
Storage Gateway
Bridge on-prem apps to S3 and Glacier.
Lifecycle
Automate transitions from S3 to archival tiers.
Explore Key Topics
Glacier vs Deep Archive
Trade retrieval time for lower storage cost; choose based on access frequency.
Storage Gateway Types
File, Volume, and Tape Gateways serve different on‑premises needs without app changes.
Lifecycle Policies
Automate transitions and expirations to keep costs predictable and compliant.

screens.title: Why archival storage exists
screens.narratorSegment: Archival storage is a deliberate trade-off: enormous durability and low storage cost in exchange for slower, sometimes delayed access. The key idea is matching how you use data to the storage economics. Regulatory or compliance data is often read rarely but must be kept intact for years. Media archives and research outputs may be accessed very infrequently but cannot be lost. Services like S3 Glacier and Glacier Deep Archive are designed for these scenarios with extremely low cost per gigabyte and very high durability, stated as eleven nines. When you choose an archival tier you consider three things: how often you will retrieve the data, how fast you need it when you do, and how important storage cost is to your budget. A common mistake is archiving actively accessed datasets; that can cause high retrieval charges and slow response times. A good example is a hospital storing completed patient records for ten years — access is rare and occasional retrievals can be planned, so Deep Archive or Glacier is appropriate. Always ask: would the application tolerate hours or days to get the data back? If yes, archival tiers reduce cost dramatically. Consider data classification and retention policies before you move data to Glacier.

keyIdea.text: Archival tiers trade immediate accessibility for very low cost and extreme durability; match tier to access frequency and required retrieval time.

content.html:
Core Concept › Why archival storage exists

Durability and cost shape archival choices

Not all data needs instant access. Archival storage reduces cost while maintaining durability for long retention needs.

Definition & key properties
  • High durability (eleven nines) and encryption at rest for long retention.
  • Very low cost per GB; designed for infrequent access patterns.
  • Retrieval times are intentionally longer and come with distinct pricing.
Analogy
Think of Glacier like an offsite archive room: secure and cheap to store boxes, but it takes time to fetch a specific box.
Example & takeaway
Example: A research lab stores raw experiment data for 15 years. Access is rare; Deep Archive reduces cost while meeting retention rules.
Key Takeaway
Match access needs to tier to avoid surprising retrieval cost.
Common Mistake
Archiving frequently accessed data and paying high retrieval fees.

screens.title: S3 Glacier retrieval options
screens.narratorSegment: Retrieval options in S3 Glacier are central to planning cost and response time. There are three documented choices: Expedited, Standard, and Bulk. Expedited retrievals return data in one to five minutes and are the most expensive; they are appropriate only when you need urgent access to a small archive. Standard retrievals typically take three to five hours and balance cost and speed for routine restores. Bulk retrievals are intended for large-scale restores and can take five to twelve hours; they are the cheapest option per gigabyte but the slowest. When you design a workflow, estimate both how often restores will be requested and how quickly users can wait. For example, a media firm might use expedited retrieval for an urgent file needed for same‑day broadcasting, while large film archives would use bulk retrieval for scheduled transfers. A common misconception is assuming expedited is cheap because it’s fast; in fact, frequent expedited restores defeat the cost benefits of archiving. Finally, remember Glacier Deep Archive offers even longer retrieval windows with its own standard and bulk options, so plan retrieval frequency across tiers to control cost.

keyIdea.text: Pick retrieval option based on urgency and volume: expedited for urgent, standard for normal, bulk for large cheap restores.

content.html:
Process Flow › Glacier Retrieval Options

Expedited, Standard, Bulk

Each option defines typical retrieval time and cost characteristics. Choose based on urgency and volume.

1
Expedited Retrieval
Typical time: 1–5 minutes. Use when you need urgent access to a small amount of data. Most expensive per gigabyte. Best for emergency restores or last-minute production needs.
2
Standard Retrieval
Typical time: 3–5 hours. Balanced cost and speed. Suitable for scheduled restores that need results the same day.
3
Bulk Retrieval
Typical time: 5–12 hours. Designed for large restores where cost is the priority. Cheapest per GB but slowest response.
Examples & pitfalls
Example: A broadcast producer needs a clip in 20 minutes — expedited is the right choice. Pitfall: using expedited for routine restores quickly erodes cost savings of archival storage.
Check Your Understanding
For a yearly audit where data is retrieved once, which option minimizes cost? Think about Bulk versus Deep Archive alternatives.
Key Takeaway
Urgency and data volume determine the retrieval option; plan restores to avoid expensive patterns.

screens.title: S3 Glacier Deep Archive
screens.narratorSegment: S3 Glacier Deep Archive pushes archival cost to the absolute minimum for data you rarely access — perhaps once or twice a year, or even less. It provides the same emphasis on durability and encryption at rest, while offering retrieval options with longer windows: a standard retrieval within 12 hours and bulk retrieval within 48 hours. That means Deep Archive is ideal for regulated data that must be retained for many years, such as financial records or healthcare archives, where immediate access is not required. A practical misconception to avoid is thinking Deep Archive removes retrieval costs; it reduces storage price but retrieval still incurs cost and takes time. Use Deep Archive for datasets that can accept those retrieval windows and where the cost savings across many terabytes or petabytes are significant. When you design retention policies, consider how often auditors or researchers will request data and whether scheduling bulk restores around those events is acceptable. Deep Archive is commonly paired with lifecycle policies so objects transition automatically after a defined retention period, ensuring compliance with minimal operational overhead. S3 Glacier Deep Archive means use glacier deep archive when storage cost is the primary concern and retrieval delays up to 48 hours are acceptable.. In practical terms, lowest-cost archival tier for years-long retention. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › Glacier Deep Archive

Lowest-cost long-term storage

Designed for data that is rarely accessed but must be retained for compliance or historical purposes.

Retrieval Options
Standard retrieval: within 12 hours. Bulk retrieval: within 48 hours. Use scheduling and planning for restores to keep costs low.
Use Case
Regulated financial records retained for ten years with access only for annual audits.
Practical notes
  • Deep Archive is best when retrieval frequency is extremely low.
  • Combine lifecycle rules to automate transitions from S3 to Deep Archive after a defined age.
  • Plan retrieval windows for audits and schedule bulk restores to minimize cost.
Key Takeaway
Deep Archive reduces storage cost for years-long retention, but plan retrievals carefully for audits or restores.

screens.title: Lifecycle policies: automate transitions
screens.narratorSegment: Lifecycle policies automate the process of moving objects from S3 Standard into archival tiers. This is safer and less error‑prone than manual transfers. A lifecycle rule can target all objects or a path prefix and specify when to transition current versions to Glacier or Glacier Deep Archive. For tests, you might set a transition after one day to observe behavior. The JSON structure includes Rule ID, Filter, Status, Transitions with days and storage class, and optional Expiration. A practical misconception is expecting immediate class change; the object's storage class updates per lifecycle processing, and retrieval still requires the Glacier retrieval process. Use lifecycle rules to enforce retention policies and to make archival durable and repeatable. Later you can combine lifecycle rules with object tagging to archive only specific categories of data, such as logs or completed records. Make sure lifecycle timing aligns with your compliance windows and that you understand retrieval implications before applying rules to production data. Lifecycle policies: automate transitions means lifecycle rules reliably transition objects to archival storage based on age or tags, reducing manual effort and policy drift.. In practical terms, use lifecycle rules to move s3 objects to glacier or deep archive. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process › Lifecycle Policy Example

Create a lifecycle rule to archive data

A lifecycle rule defines transitions, expiration, and scope. Use tags or prefixes to target objects safely.

Sample lifecycle JSON (simplified)
{
  "Rules": [
    {
      "ID": "ArchiveToGlacier",
      "Filter": { "Prefix": "" },
      "Status": "Enabled",
      "Transitions": [
        { "Days": 1, "StorageClass": "GLACIER" }
      ],
      "Expiration": { "Days": 30 }
    }
  ]
}
CLI: aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket your-bucket --lifecycle-configuration file://glacier-lifecycle.json
Notes and best practices
  • Test with non-critical files and short transition days to observe behavior.
  • Use tags to limit scope and avoid archiving hot data by accident.
  • Align lifecycle timing with retention and compliance requirements.
Key Takeaway
Lifecycle rules make archival repeatable and auditable; plan transitions to control retrieval cost.

Add a transition for current versions of objects to S3 Glacier after one day so you can see the storage class change rapidly in a test environment. After creating the rule, monitor the object storage class in the S3 console and plan a test retrieval to observe the retrieval workflow and pricing implications. This practice builds familiarity with lifecycle automation and helps you avoid accidental archival of production data. content.html:
Hands-on Activity › Create lifecycle policy

Configure a lifecycle rule for testing

Follow these steps in the console or use the JSON and CLI to automate transitions for test objects.

Step-by-step
  1. Create a bucket named cohortia-archive-test-bucket-yourname and upload small test files.
  2. Open Management → Lifecycle rules and click Create lifecycle rule.
  3. Name it ArchiveToGlacier and apply to all objects.
  4. Add Transition: After 1 day → Transition to S3 Glacier.
  5. Optionally add Expiration after 30 days for cleanup.
  6. Save and observe object storage class after processing.
CLI JSON & command
{
  "Rules": [
    {
      "ID": "ArchiveToGlacier",
      "Filter": { "Prefix": "" },
      "Status": "Enabled",
      "Transitions": [ { "Days": 1, "StorageClass": "GLACIER" } ],
      "Expiration": { "Days": 30 }
    }
  ]
}

# CLI (example):
aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket cohortia-archive-test-bucket-yourname --lifecycle-configuration file://glacier-lifecycle.json
Safety Note
Use non-critical files for tests. Retrieving from Glacier costs money and takes time.

screens.title: AWS Storage Gateway — hybrid storage explained
screens.narratorSegment: Hybrid cloud storage often requires keeping local performance while benefiting from cloud scalability and durability. AWS Storage Gateway does exactly that: it provides local interfaces your applications already use, while storing or backing up data in S3 or Glacier. The gateway runs on premises or in a virtual appliance and provides local caching to keep the most frequently accessed data close to the application. This reduces latency for hot data while sending cold or backup data to S3. Storage Gateway supports multiple modes to match application requirements, enabling lift-and-shift migrations, cloud backups, and long-term retention without changing the application. When designing with Storage Gateway, evaluate network connectivity and security because gateways require reliable connectivity to AWS. Also plan caching capacity so local performance targets are met. Use the gateway to modernize storage with minimal application changes: the application continues to use familiar protocols and benefits from cloud durability and lifecycle rules in S3 and Glacier for long-term archival. AWS Storage Gateway — hybrid storage explained means storage gateway offers local interfaces and caching while using s3/glacier as durable backend storage, enabling hybrid architectures without app changes.. In practical terms, bridge on-premises applications to aws storage with local caching and cloud durability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › Storage Gateway Overview

Bridge local apps to cloud storage

Storage Gateway gives familiar file or block interfaces and local caching while storing data durably in S3 and Glacier.

How it works
  • Gateway presents NFS/SMB or iSCSI interfaces to on-prem applications.
  • Data is cached locally for low-latency access to frequently used data.

screens.title: Volume Gateway — Cached vs Stored
screens.narratorSegment: Volume Gateway provides iSCSI block volumes to on‑premises applications and comes in two modes: Cached and Stored. Cached Volumes keep the primary dataset in S3 while a cache of frequently accessed blocks stays on‑premises. This mode is ideal when you want cloud scalability and keep only a hot working set locally to meet latency needs. Stored Volumes keep the entire primary dataset on‑premises and back it up asynchronously to S3 as snapshots; this mode suits applications that require low-latency access to the full dataset locally while still benefiting from durable, offsite backups. A common confusion is thinking both modes provide identical local performance; Stored Volumes provide full local dataset access while Cached Volumes may require network access for cold blocks. Use Cached Volumes to reduce local storage footprint and Stored Volumes when application latency demands local access to all data. In both cases, snapshots to S3 let you restore or archive to Glacier later via lifecycle rules, giving a hybrid backup and archival path without changing application block storage APIs. Design › Cost-effective archival strategy

A practical checklist

Follow these steps to design archival that meets retention and cost goals.

Steps
  1. Classify data by retention and access frequency.
  2. Map classes to Glacier or Deep Archive using retrieval windows as a guide.
  3. Choose retrieval options and schedule restores for audits.
  4. Automate with lifecycle rules and object tagging.
  5. Pick Storage Gateway type if on-premises integration is required and model costs including possible restores.
Example scenario
An enterprise must retain financial records for ten years with rare audit access. Classification puts these records in Deep Archive. Use lifecycle rules to transition records after a retention period, and schedule bulk retrievals for audits. Estimate storage plus expected single annual retrieval cost to confirm Deep Archive with Bulk retrieval is most cost-effective.
Key Takeaway
Model both storage and retrieval across the retention window; retrieval frequency can be the dominant cost factor if overlooked.

Third, use Storage Gateway to bridge on‑premises applications to S3 and archival tiers without reengineering; choose File, Volume, or Tape Gateway based on the application interface. These concepts let you produce architectures that meet compliance, control cost, and preserve application behavior. Before finalizing any design, model both storage cost and expected retrieval cost over the retention period and run a lifecycle test in a sandbox bucket. That practice helps you avoid common mistakes like archiving active data or underestimating retrieval expenses.

fullNarratorScript:
Long-term archival is about durability, cost, and the right retrieval expectations. In this lesson you will learn why services like S3 Glacier and Glacier Deep Archive exist, when to accept slower retrieval in exchange for much lower storage cost, and how Storage Gateway helps you connect on-premises applications to the cloud without rewriting them. We will compare retrieval options, show a lifecycle policy example you can use for testing, and walk through the three Storage Gateway types — File, Volume, and Tape — with concrete scenarios. You will also practice designing an archival approach that balances compliance, access patterns, and cost. As you explore, keep in mind a simple rule: match the storage tier to how often you need the data and how quickly you need it. By the end, you will be able to recommend Glacier, Glacier Deep Archive, or a Storage Gateway configuration based on a real retention or application requirement. Think about a dataset you manage now: how often do you need to restore it, and what retrieval delay would be acceptable?

These objectives orient your study and link what you practice to measurable competency. First, you'll identify when to use S3 Glacier versus Glacier Deep Archive by matching access frequency and retention length to retrieval options and cost. Second, you'll explain retrieval options — expedited, standard, and bulk — and how they trade speed for price in Glacier, and the standard and bulk options in Deep Archive. Third, you'll describe how AWS Storage Gateway creates a hybrid storage architecture, including file, volume, and tape gateways, and why each matches common on‑premises needs. Fourth, you'll design a simple archival strategy that uses lifecycle rules to automate transitions and balances retrieval cost, retention policies, and compliance. Each objective has a direct milestone: being able to choose a storage class for a given retention requirement, to write a lifecycle rule sample, and to select the correct gateway type for an unmodified application. As you learn, consider a compliance example — a 10‑year retention audit — and practice mapping that requirement to Deep Archive and a bulk retrieval approach.

Now let's attach short practice actions and visual mnemonics to each objective so you can reliably demonstrate competency. For identifying Glacier tiers, use the mnemonic 'Access Frequency then Retention Length' — ask how often you will retrieve the data and how long you must keep it. For retrieval options, practice choosing between Expedited, Standard, and Bulk using a simple rule: urgency dictates cost. For Storage Gateway, map the application interface to gateway type: file shares map to File Gateway, block volumes to Volume Gateway, and legacy tape backups to Tape Gateway. For designing an archival strategy, practice writing one lifecycle rule that transitions test objects to Glacier after a day and expires them later; this both tests lifecycle behavior and reminds you to consider retrieval cost. These micro-exercises let you show, not just tell, that you understand the concepts. After each, confirm your choice by stating why a faster retrieval would increase cost and when Deep Archive's longer delays are acceptable.

Archival storage is a deliberate trade-off: enormous durability and low storage cost in exchange for slower, sometimes delayed access. The key idea is matching how you use data to the storage economics. Regulatory or compliance data is often read rarely but must be kept intact for years. Media archives and research outputs may be accessed very infrequently but cannot be lost. Services like S3 Glacier and Glacier Deep Archive are designed for these scenarios with extremely low cost per gigabyte and very high durability, stated as eleven nines. When you choose an archival tier you consider three things: how often you will retrieve the data, how fast you need it when you do, and how important storage cost is to your budget. A common mistake is archiving actively accessed datasets; that can cause high retrieval charges and slow response times. A good example is a hospital storing completed patient records for ten years — access is rare and occasional retrievals can be planned, so Deep Archive or Glacier is appropriate. Always ask: would the application tolerate hours or days to get the data back? If yes, archival tiers reduce cost dramatically. Consider data classification and retention policies before you move data to Glacier.

Retrieval options in S3 Glacier are central to planning cost and response time. There are three documented choices: Expedited, Standard, and Bulk. Expedited retrievals return data in one to five minutes and are the most expensive; they are appropriate only when you need urgent access to a small archive. Standard retrievals typically take three to five hours and balance cost and speed for routine restores. Bulk retrievals are intended for large-scale restores and can take five to twelve hours; they are the cheapest option per gigabyte but the slowest. When you design a workflow, estimate both how often restores will be requested and how quickly users can wait. For example, a media firm might use expedited retrieval for an urgent file needed for same‑day broadcasting, while large film archives would use bulk retrieval for scheduled transfers. A common misconception is assuming expedited is cheap because it’s fast; in fact, frequent expedited restores defeat the cost benefits of archiving. Finally, remember Glacier Deep Archive offers even longer retrieval windows with its own standard and bulk options, so plan retrieval frequency across tiers to control cost.

S3 Glacier Deep Archive pushes archival cost to the absolute minimum for data you rarely access — perhaps once or twice a year, or even less. It provides the same emphasis on durability and encryption at rest, while offering retrieval options with longer windows: a standard retrieval within 12 hours and bulk retrieval within 48 hours. That means Deep Archive is ideal for regulated data that must be retained for many years, such as financial records or healthcare archives, where immediate access is not required. A practical misconception to avoid is thinking Deep Archive removes retrieval costs; it reduces storage price but retrieval still incurs cost and takes time. Use Deep Archive for datasets that can accept those retrieval windows and where the cost savings across many terabytes or petabytes are significant. When you design retention policies, consider how often auditors or researchers will request data and whether scheduling bulk restores around those events is acceptable. Deep Archive is commonly paired with lifecycle policies so objects transition automatically after a defined retention period, ensuring compliance with minimal operational overhead. S3 Glacier Deep Archive means use glacier deep archive when storage cost is the primary concern and retrieval delays up to 48 hours are acceptable.. In practical terms, lowest-cost archival tier for years-long retention. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Lifecycle policies automate the process of moving objects from S3 Standard into archival tiers. This is safer and less error‑prone than manual transfers. A lifecycle rule can target all objects or a path prefix and specify when to transition current versions to Glacier or Glacier Deep Archive. For tests, you might set a transition after one day to observe behavior. The JSON structure includes Rule ID, Filter, Status, Transitions with days and storage class, and optional Expiration. A practical misconception is expecting immediate class change; the object's storage class updates per lifecycle processing, and retrieval still requires the Glacier retrieval process. Use lifecycle rules to enforce retention policies and to make archival durable and repeatable. Later you can combine lifecycle rules with object tagging to archive only specific categories of data, such as logs or completed records. Make sure lifecycle timing aligns with your compliance windows and that you understand retrieval implications before applying rules to production data. In practical terms, use lifecycle rules to move s3 objects to glacier or deep archive. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This hands-on activity walks you through creating a lifecycle rule for a test bucket. Start by creating a new S3 bucket and upload small, non-critical files so you can safely observe transitions. In the S3 console under Management, create a lifecycle rule called ArchiveToGlacier that applies to all objects. Add a transition for current versions of objects to S3 Glacier after one day so you can see the storage class change rapidly in a test environment. Optionally set an expiration after thirty days for cleanup. The supplied JSON shows the essential fields: ID, Filter, Status, Transitions with Days and StorageClass, and Expiration. AWS Storage Gateway does exactly that: it provides local interfaces your applications already use, while storing or backing up data in S3 or Glacier. The gateway runs on premises or in a virtual appliance and provides local caching to keep the most frequently accessed data close to the application. This reduces latency for hot data while sending cold or backup data to S3. When an application writes files to the gateway, the files are stored as objects in S3 and a local cache holds frequently accessed data. This makes File Gateway ideal for migrating file shares or integrating on‑premises file workflows with cloud processing without modifying the application.
